newsitem.title: USA: Asia, Latin America seen boosting U.S. ag exports.
newsitem.headline: Asia, Latin America seen boosting U.S. ag exports.

text.p: Fast-growing Asian and Latin American economies promise good markets for U.S. farm exports for the next several years, but global competition for those markets will be intense, a senior farm official told grain industry leaders Friday.

"Asia and Latin American regions will be the key growth areas. ... There is opportunity there, but we'll have to work very hard against competitors," said Chris Goldthwait, general sales manager for the Agriculture Department.

Goldthwait told attendees of the annual meeting of the National Grain and Feed Association that the government's goal is for U.S. farm exports to increase by 50 percent by the year 2000, to $65 billion worth. He said that, despite the challenges, "we're on track to that goal."

Goldthwait said that, while many of the big traditional markets of U.S. farm goods -- especially Japan, South Korea and Europe -- have stabilised, income growth and an increasing appetite for meat and other high-value foods in such countries as China, Indonesia, Mexico and Brazil will spur U.S. farm shipments for some time.

China is the fastest growing economy in the world, and although the "extraordinary" growth of the last 10 to 15 years may taper off, the Agriculture Department official said that country is still likely to be a big player in the U.S. market.
Mexico bought a record amount of American grains and other farm goods this past year, and government analysts estimate its appetite could increase another 10 percent in 1997.

Goldthwait said that U.S. agricultural exports to South America in general, which had dropped off in the past few years, have shown a remarkable recovery and are approaching the record levels set in the early 1980s.
Outside of Asia and Latin America, other developing economies are also beginning to lap up U.S. goods.

Russia, a huge importer of American grain before the collapse of the Communist government, has returned to the U.S. markets and is now the No. 1 importer of U.S. poultry. Goldthwait noted a lot of grain is now moving to Russia in the form of corn-fed chickens.
North Africa, the Middle East and the former Soviet bloc countries also hold big potential for the U.S. grain industry.
But Goldthwait noted that increased crop production in major competing nations such as Canada, Australia, the European Union and Argentina, will give American farmers a run for their money.
"We'll need to work very hard to maintain our market share," said Goldthwait. "The markets will be subject to intense competition."
